newsitem.title: USA: Netanyahu wants end to 'one-way Israeli giving'.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu wants end to 'one-way Israeli giving'.

text.p: As thousands of Palestinians greeted Yasser Arafat in Hebron on Sunday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu indicated he wanted the PLO to begin fulfilling its peace commitments.

Speaking on American television, Netanyahu said for the peace process to continue there had to be an end to Israel's "one-way giving." He also said he hoped to resume peace talks with Syria but indicated no change of stance over the disputed Golan Heights.

"We now have a blueprint on how to proceed (with the PLO). If we are going to proceed then we have got to end the situation of one-way giving by Israel and one-way receiving by the Palestinians. We fulfil our commitments, they fulfil theirs," Netanyahu said on 'Fox News Sunday' television programme.

"It is not only Israel that has to keep it's side of the agreement like the Hebron redeployment. But the Palestinian side has to keep their side of the agreement like annulling the PLO charter that calls for Israel's destruction."
He said on ABC's "This Week" programme that "a measure of compliance on one side should mean a measure of compliance on the other side."

The Israeli Prime Minister told CNN that a strong Israeli-U.S. partnership was vital to ensuring peace in the Middle East and said the Clinton administration had a role to play in helping resurrect peace talks with Syria.

"Our part of the world is still unstable ... it requires a major effort to produce peace. The most important element of stability in the Middle East is a strong Israel and a strong American-Israeli alliance," Netanyahu said.
"If you have that, all the other pieces fall into place. The special bond, special relationship Israel has with the U.S. ... these are the axis of stability in the Middle East."

Netanyahu, in his first American television interviews since Israel and the PLO concluded a long-elusive agreement on Wednesday extending Palestinian rule to Hebron in the West Bank, said his government had not changed its stance on Jerusalem.
As Arafat laid claim to Hebron in a speech to 25,000 supporters on a hill above the city on Sunday, he promised to make Arab East Jerusalem his capital.
"A promise is a promise, we will continue to Jerusalem," he said.
Netanyahu said: "He can seek all he wants. We are not going to re-divide Jerusalem. We are not going to erect a Berlin Wall in the centre of that city again.
"We want to see a unified Jerusalem and Israel with proper defences. We offer self-government to Palestinians but not with sovereign powers that can threaten the state of Israel," he added.
Netanyahu said contacts had begun with Syria, through U.S. channels, in seeking to resume peace talks.

He said the United States had always played a critical role in more difficult peace negotiations between Israel and its Arab neighbours and that once the new administration was in place it would have a "pivotal role" there as well.
"Peace is important for Syria as it is important for us. It's important for their children and our children. If this is the guiding principle we should be able to resume the talks," he said.

Talks have been blocked over the fate of the Golan Heights, which Israel seized from Syria in the 1967 Middle East war. Syria demands a full Israeli withdrawal in exchange for peace. Netanyahu also wants all of the strategic plateau.
"The Golan Heights is a very important piece of real estate for us. It gives us the protection against any future attack," he said on Fox TV.
"Peace is not just a piece of paper you sign and forget about. Peace is kept by the ability to enforce the peace and the Golan Heights is very important for Israel's defence."
